newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Key players in Dutch EU presidency.
newsitem.headline: Key players in Dutch EU presidency.

text.p: The Netherlands' low-key approach to its presidency of the European Union reflects the character of its leadership -- a left-right coalition based more on consensus politics than party-political ideology.
The three key players who will determine whether the presidency succeeds span the Dutch political spectrum, but are joined in their support of deeper European integration.
Unlike 1991, when attempts by then Dutch premier Ruud Lubbers to set a seal on Europe were sharply rebuffed, this term will focus on finishing the task handed on by Ireland.

Observers note that this "modesty offensive" fits with Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok's political style. While he may lack Lubbers' colour and spark, his arguments are cogent and well-supported, commentators say.
"The (Dutch) approach is more sober, less inflated than last time," one Dutch MP said recently. "That's in keeping with Kok. Lubbers tended towards more Sun King-like views."
Kok, Labour Party (PvdA) leader since 1986 and a former trade union boss and finance minister, became the Netherlands' third socialist prime minister in 1994.
Heading a tripartite coalition of Labour, reformist D66 and conservative Liberals VVD, Kok has won wide respect with his quiet brand of statesmanship and prudent financial management.
Opinion polls show seven in 10 Dutch would welcome a second term, seeing the no-nonsense Kok as a reliable pair of hands.
Internationally, Kok is seen as a sharp-witted and able negotiator whose lack of ego allows him to forge compromises where others might fail.

As finance minister in the early 1990s he was instrumental in taking an axe to the Netherlands' top-heavy welfare system, putting the country on the road to lower deficits and bolstering the guilder, now one of Europe's strongest currencies.
While alienating some of Labour's traditional voters, it won him the confidence of the private sector and enabled him to shake off the leftist tax-and-spend tag.

Under his premiership the Dutch are strong on budgetary discipline and were among the most fervent supporters of German proposals for a stability pact to ensure continued adherence to convergence criteria after Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).

Kok enjoys warmer relations with German Chancellor Helmut Kohl than did Lubbers, but ties with French President Jacques Chirac are strained. Kok uncharacteristically called Chirac "unbalanced" when it came to discussing Dutch drugs policy.
Although a political veteran, Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo is a relative newcomer to government. The D66 leader briefly served as defence minister in the early 1980s.
A former journalist, Van Mierlo is acknowledged as an inspired orator with a talent for the soundbite. For many Dutch, Van Mierlo adds the colour that Kok lacks.
"Van Mierlo's feel for timing and atmosphere can act as a counterpoint to Kok's more distant and rational approach," one observer said recently.

But the genial Van Mierlo is not renowned for doing his homework. "...complicated dossiers (are) not his greatest love," daily NRC Handelsblad said recently, adding that as defence minister "his in-tray was always fuller than his out-tray."
As chairman of the group negotiating the inter-governmental conference (IGC), deputy foreign minister Michiel Patijn will be responsible for rounding off landmark treaty reforms.
Patijn, a Labour defector to the VVD, has been called a Euro sceptic, although he points out that he is not a sceptic in the British sense.
"I am sceptical out of a sense of Euro-loyalty...I don't think it serves the cause of Europe to make exaggerated claims about what Europe can achieve," he said in a recent interview.

Scion of a political dynasty -- his brother is mayor of Amsterdam and his father and grandfather were MPs -- Patijn's civil service career spans development, economic affairs and defence plus a stint in the Dutch embassy in Washington.
